title: The Empty Tomb and the Risen Jesus

verses.text: Early on the first day of the week, while it was still dark, Mary Magdalene went to the tomb and saw that the stone had been removed from the entrance.
So she came running to Simon Peter and the other disciple, the one whom Jesus loved. "They have taken the Lord out of the tomb," she said, "and we do not know where they have put Him!"
Then Peter and the other disciple set out for the tomb.
The two were running together, but the other disciple outran Peter and reached the tomb first.
He bent down and looked in at the linen cloths lying there, but he did not go in.
Simon Peter arrived just after him. He entered the tomb and saw the linen cloths lying there.
The cloth that had been around Jesus' head was rolled up, lying separate from the linen cloths.
Then the other disciple, who had reached the tomb first, also went in. And he saw and believed.
For they still did not understand from the Scripture that Jesus had to rise from the dead.
Then the disciples returned to their homes.
But Mary stood outside the tomb weeping. And as she wept, she bent down to look into the tomb,
and she saw two angels in white sitting where the body of Jesus had lain, one at the head and the other at the feet.
"Woman, why are you weeping?" they asked. "Because they have taken my Lord away," she said, "and I do not know where they have put Him."
When she had said this, she turned around and saw Jesus standing there. But she did not recognize that it was Jesus.
"Woman, why are you weeping?" Jesus asked. "Whom are you seeking?" Thinking He was the gardener, she said, "Sir, if you have carried Him off, tell me where you have put Him, and I will get Him."
Jesus said to her, "Mary." She turned and said to Him in Hebrew, "Rabboni!" (which means "Teacher").
"Do not cling to Me," Jesus said, "for I have not yet ascended to the Father. But go and tell My brothers, 'I am ascending to My Father and your Father, to My God and your God.'"
Mary Magdalene went and announced to the disciples, "I have seen the Lord!" And she told them what He had said to her.

It was the first day of the week, and that very evening, while the disciples were together with the doors locked for fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood among them. "Peace be with you!" He said to them.
After He had said this, He showed them His hands and His side. The disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord.
Again Jesus said to them, "Peace be with you. As the Father has sent Me, so also I am sending you."
When He had said this, He breathed on them and said, "Receive the Holy Spirit.
If you forgive anyone his sins, they are forgiven; if you withhold forgiveness from anyone, it is withheld."
Now Thomas called Didymus, one of the Twelve, was not with the disciples when Jesus came.

So the other disciples told him, "We have seen the Lord!" But he replied, "Unless I see the nail marks in His hands, and put my finger where the nails have been, and put my hand into His side, I will never believe."
Eight days later, His disciples were once again inside with the doors locked, and Thomas was with them. Jesus came and stood among them and said, "Peace be with you."
Then Jesus said to Thomas, "Put your finger here and look at My hands. Reach out your hand and put it into My side. Stop doubting and believe."
Thomas replied, "My Lord and my God!"
Jesus said to him, "Because you have seen Me, you have believed; blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed."
Jesus performed many other signs in the presence of His disciples, which are not written in this book.
But these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in His name.

context.author: Traditionally the apostle John
context.genre: Historical narrative — the resurrection accounts, closing with the purpose statement John gives for the whole book in verses 30-31
context.audience: A broad, likely mixed Jewish and Gentile readership toward the end of the first century
context.setting: The chapter begins at the new rock-cut tomb in the garden near Golgotha, where Jesus was buried at the end of chapter 19, and moves to a locked room in Jerusalem, probably the same city quarter where the disciples had been staying. First-century tombs of this type were closed with a large disc-shaped stone rolled across the entrance.
context.custom: A body was wrapped in strips of linen with spices, and the face covered with a separate cloth. John's note that the head cloth was rolled up and lying apart is often read as showing an orderly scene rather than hurried theft. In this culture a woman's testimony carried little weight in legal settings, yet all four Gospels report women as the first witnesses.
context.timelineImmediate: Everything in the chapter happens within about eight days: the empty tomb before dawn on the first day of the week, Jesus' appearance to Mary Magdalene that morning, His appearance to the disciples that evening, and then Thomas's encounter a week later. The last two verses step back and tell the reader why John wrote any of it.
context.timelineBible: John's Greek for "the first day of the week" is literally "the first of the Sabbaths" — a way of counting the days from one Sabbath to the next. Jesus breathing on His disciples recalls God breathing life into Adam in Genesis 2:7, and His commission "as the Father has sent Me, so also I am sending you" picks up His prayer from chapter 17.
context.sparkNotes: Mary Magdalene finds the tomb open and runs to tell Peter and the beloved disciple, who race there and find the grave cloths lying inside; the beloved disciple sees and believes. Mary, lingering in tears, mistakes Jesus for the gardener until He speaks her name. That evening Jesus appears to the disciples behind locked doors, shows them His hands and side, commissions them, and breathes on them. A week later He invites doubting Thomas to touch His wounds, drawing the confession "My Lord and my God!" John then states his purpose: these things are written so readers may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and have life in His name.

translation.meaning: Literally "one of the Sabbaths" — the standard way of naming the day after the Sabbath. It is the same phrase used in all four Gospel accounts of the empty tomb.
An Aramaic form of "Rabbi" that John translates for his readers as "Teacher." It is a deeply personal address, and it is the moment of recognition: Mary knows Him only when He says her name.

Some early manuscripts have a tense that means "come to believe," others a tense that means "continue to believe," which is why the Berean Standard Bible footnotes this verse. Either way, John states that the whole book exists to lead to faith that brings life.

gospelParallels.note: Matthew's account of the women at the empty tomb and the angel's message.
Mark's account of the women finding the open tomb.
Mark's brief account of Jesus appearing first to Mary Magdalene (this passage appears in the longer ending of Mark, whose manuscript history is noted in Mark 16).

otBackground.note: God's Holy One will not see decay — quoted in the apostles' later preaching as pointing to the resurrection.
God breathing life into Adam — echoed when Jesus breathes on His disciples.
Revival and raising up "on the third day" — often connected by readers to the timing of the resurrection.

commentary.note: Henry makes a point about why the resurrection matters to the whole transaction: "if Christ gave his life a ransom, and had not taken it again, it would not have appeared that his giving it was accepted as satisfaction." On John's closing verses, he says the other signs were left unwritten so that all might believe Jesus is the promised Messiah and, by that faith, obtain eternal life.

Ellicott draws attention to the eyewitness detail in verses 6-7: Peter "beholds" the linen cloths with a different, more careful Greek verb than John uses when he only sees them from outside. Of the head cloth folded in a separate place, he says it reaches the climax of "the minute knowledge and remembrance of an eye-witness" — the fact that it was folded "did not escape the writer's eye, nor fade from his memory."

Wesley reads "do not cling to me" as a gentle "detain me not now" to Mary, who was holding His feet, with more opportunities to come. He sees the message "go to my brothers" as an unspoken forgiveness, since Jesus never mentions the disciples' failure. On Thomas, he notes he confesses Jesus' divinity "more explicitly than any other had yet done," and without ever touching the wounds.

overview.summary: On Sunday morning Mary Magdalene finds the stone moved, and Peter and John run to the empty tomb. Jesus appears to Mary, to the disciples, and a week later to Thomas, who says my Lord and my God. John says these things are written so you may believe.
overview.settingLine: The garden tomb, then a locked room.

history.t: The disciples hid, since the Jewish leaders had just had Jesus executed.
Mary Magdalene, whose word was not valued in court, is the first to see Him.

customs.t: Burial cloths and a separate face cloth lay neatly in the tomb.
Rock-cut tombs were sealed with a heavy stone, so rolling it away took strength.

archaeology.t: Rock-cut tombs with rolling stones are found around Jerusalem.
The church marks the tomb site honored since the fourth century.

overview.discussion: Jesus said, "Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed." What does believing without seeing look like?
overview.book: The fourth Gospel · 21 chapters. Written so readers would believe Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God.
overview.author: John
